    Europe Steps Into the Breach on Ukraine

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1210 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival.
    • According to recent reports, the Trump administration has, since the start of its second term, been implacably hostile to Kyiv, from Oval Office beatdowns to a relaxation of sanctions on Russia to demands that Ukraine desist from carrying out long-range strikes against Russian oil facilities.
    • Now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    Understanding the conflict four years in.

    Sources indicate that now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival. This week will be crucial, with the European Council meeting on Nov. 26-27 to decide on an additional loan of 45 billion euros (about $49.5 billion) to tide Ukraine over next year as it wrestles with nonstop missile strikes, jet-powered drones, and a gaping hole in its budget.

    According to recent reports, the Trump administration has, since the start of its second term, been implacably hostile to Kyiv, from Oval Office beatdowns to a relaxation of sanctions on Russia to demands that Ukraine desist from carrying out long-range strikes against Russian oil facilities. That hostility, like the war, has only escalated, with U.S. President Donald Trump suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports (in a bid to lower fuel prices) and neutering the latest legislation meant to economically punish Moscow.

    Now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival. This week will be crucial, with the European Council meeting on Nov. 26-27 to decide on an additional loan of 45 billion euros (about $49.5 billion) to tide Ukraine over next year as it wrestles with nonstop missile strikes, jet-powered drones, and a gaping hole in its budget.

    The Trump administration has, since the start of its second term, been implacably hostile to Kyiv, from Oval Office beatdowns to a relaxation of sanctions on Russia to demands that Ukraine desist from carrying out long-range strikes against Russian oil facilities. That hostility, like the war, has only escalated, with U.S. President Donald Trump suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports (in a bid to lower fuel prices) and neutering the latest legislation meant to economically punish Moscow.

    According to recent reports, “It began with the diesel deal. This is the longest sustained effort by Team Trump” to put its thumb on the scales, mentioned John Herbst, a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine. “It annoys me even more that they are helping [Russian President Vladimir] Putin do this. Putin wants to undermine NATO, and that is why it is so frustrating.”.

    Trump had previously adumbrated his approach to Ukraine by delaying approval of the bipartisan legislation, championed by former Sen. Lindsey Graham, that would have levied stiff tariffs on Russia’s trading partners and put additional sanctions on top Russian officials. When the legislation finally did pass, Trump watered it down, waiving the sanctions and for once forgetting about tariffs.

    According to recent reports, “I found U.S. policy over the last six weeks depressing,” said Steven Pifer, another former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine. “I think Trump is lost to the cause, even if the American people are not.”.

    In a recent development, now it falls to Europe to fill the gap, both in terms of Kyiv’s budget and its defense needs. About half of the new loan is earmarked for Ukraine’s administration and the other half for defense procurement.

    According to recent reports, the European loan is not a done deal. There are four holdouts among the usual suspects—Hungary, Slovakia, Bulgaria, and the Czech Republic—that are leery of signing onto more blocwide debt to support a country they view askance. But by Friday, informed observers say, the European Union will probably be able to hammer through a fresh 45 billion on top of the 90 billion euro loan for Ukraine that it is still doling out.

    European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has stated the latest loan would be backed by frozen Russian assets held in Europe. Those central bank assets total about $300 billion worldwide, with just over $200 billion in Belgium. Despite years of posturing, four years into the war, neither Europe nor the United States nor the United Kingdom has moved from freezing to seizing, fearful of the potential legal, financial, and other consequences of grabbing illicit Russian money. That makes the ultimate collateral for this latest European loan something of a question mark.

    “Europe has no choice but to fund Ukraine’s defense. The question is how you do it,” said Timothy Ash, a Russia expert at Chatham House. “I find it incredible, when you put it across like this, which taxpayers should pay for this: Europe’s or Russia’s?” (He has some thoughts.).

    In a recent development, the bigger question is broader. Europe knows that enabling Ukraine to survive the war, or at least avoid a dishonorable peace, is critical to the country’s survival as well as its own. The problem, which has been apparent since January 2025, is that Ukraine and Europe are on their own. The United States has not provided any fresh financial support for Kyiv since Trump came back to office, has at times interrupted intelligence-sharing and satellite links, and continues to block the sale of much-need missile interceptors held in European inventories.

    Industry observers note that U.S. Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge Colby scolded Ukraine last week for striking Russian oil facilities, arguing that such attacks were ineffective. (Ukraine’s long-range strikes have taken offline about half of Russia’s refinery capacity in recent months, cratered its energy exports, and are leading to lines at gas stations in Russia.) Meanwhile, Russian missiles and drones continue to rain down on Kyiv, Kharkiv, and other major cities.

    “Trump is just defending Putin and making it harder for Ukraine to defend itself,” Herbst remarked.

    Germany’s vocal support for mobilizing hundreds of billions of Moscow’s reserves could be a game-changer for Ukraine.

    For all the talk of a new world order, the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting produced little of substance.

    One question that looms now is whether Europe’s determination to support Ukraine—Europe has already provided nearly 240 billion euros (about $260 billion), far more than the United States or any other country—will push Trump into reprisal mode. He has in the past slapped tariffs on Europe while waiving penalties on Russia. Over the weekend, Trump posted a photo of himself with Putin titled, simply, “My Friend.”.

    It has been revealed that “If Trump wants to go down that route, it might get ugly in Europe, but I don’t think Europe can afford to let Ukraine lose. There is a real understanding in Europe about how high the stakes are for them,” Ash stated.

    In a recent development, “It will be interesting to see where this goes in terms of the U.S.-EU relationship. This could be a huge crisis. We have to see how far he is willing to take this.”.

    #122613. Latest Update: The World’s Last Chance for Peace

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3974 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: The World’s Last Chance for Peace

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3974 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.
    • It has been revealed that at some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable.
    • In a recent development, nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.

    It has been revealed that at some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable. Wars of aggression, from Ukraine to Lebanon to Iran, are on the rise, bringing horror, ruin, and the specter of a wider international confrontation. Governments increasingly treat war as something to budget and prepare for. Military spending is climbing, technological and arms races are intensifying, and more and more countries are considering whether they should acquire a nuclear deterrent to guarantee their security.

    In a recent development, nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war. It represents a return to a norm that persisted for most of human history, when war was the main organizing principle of the international system. Armed conflict was the natural way for states to settle disputes or enlarge their territory at the expense of weaker neighbors.

    In a recent development, yet the vast wreckage of World Wars I and II in the first half of the twentieth century made the status quo unacceptable. Countries united behind an effort to turn war from a legitimate instrument of statecraft into an outlawed act. Wars did not end in 1945, but for years after they were overwhelmingly condemned by the international community.

    Sources indicate that in recent decades, however, governments’ commitment to the cause of peace has weakened. Millions of people took to the streets in hundreds of cities to oppose the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, but the war proceeded nonetheless. Fought on false premises and in violation of international law, it brought destruction to Iraq, fed regional instability, and fueled resentment and terrorism directed at Western countries. The conflict also marked a turning point. Ever since, the pursuit of peace has steadily receded from the international agenda amid deepening geopolitical competition and inattention or indifference to the multilateral efforts that for decades discouraged acts of war.

    At the end of this path lies another world war—the catastrophe the twentieth-century order was designed to prevent. With that dire future looming, governments must relearn the art of opposing war. It is the responsibility of every country, including my own, Spain, to take direct action that constrains others’ ability to wage war and to strengthen the international institutions that will serve as guarantors of peace.

    It has been revealed that the success of this project will depend on an expansive multilateralism that I call “maxilateralism”—cooperation that embraces as many countries as possible, rather than being limited to small, ad hoc groupings. Its ambition is to make war increasingly impractical, even unimaginable. In 2003, protesters across Spain chanted “No a la guerra!’’—“No to war!” The world cannot afford to ignore them again.

    According to recent reports, international efforts to reject war as an instrument of national policy date back to the Kellogg–Briand Pact of 1928, a treaty signed in Paris by 15 countries and joined by dozens more later. It was insufficient to prevent World War II, but it planted a seed. When representatives of 50 countries gathered in San Francisco in 1945 to create the United Nations, they revived the spirit and principles of Kellogg–Briand and gave them what they had lacked: institutional form. The UN Charter prohibited the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of another state. And, unlike its 1928 predecessor, it backed up the prohibition with institutions empowered to enforce it.

    Recent findings suggest that in the decades that followed, these institutions established an order that penalized violations and created incentives for diplomacy and cooperation. At the same time, public opposition to war was growing stronger around the world. Popular defiance of Cold War militarism was visible in worldwide resistance to the Vietnam War and in mass movements against nuclear weapons. Pacifism reached its high-water mark in the 1990s, when a vibrant global civil society mobilized to defend humanitarian causes and when the United Nations held sufficient authority to champion a sweeping peace agenda.

    Today, however, there is more armed conflict than at any time since 1946. According to the Uppsala Conflict Data Program, there were 65 active conflicts involving governments in 2025, double the number in 2010. An estimated 250,000 people died in those conflicts—the highest annual death toll in 30 years, since the Rwandan genocide. Close to 120 million people worldwide have been forcibly displaced by war.

    Sources indicate that worryingly, wars of aggression—which violate the UN Charter—are back. Russia invaded Ukraine. The United States and Israel attacked Iran. And as fighting continues year after year in places such as Lebanon, Sudan, and Yemen, it is becoming clear that war is being accepted as a normal occurrence.

    Industry observers note that there is no sign of the trend slowing down. Military budgets have surged to levels not seen in generations, at the expense of social and development spending. In the past decade alone, global defense spending has increased by more than 40 percent, with many countries doubling their military budgets. The nearly $3 trillion the world spends annually on defense is close to the GDP of the entire African continent. Even countries with a long tradition of military restraint, such as Denmark, Germany, Japan, and Norway, are rearming rapidly. Some are reviving military service programs.

    It has been revealed that A renewed threat of nuclear war is cause for still greater dread. All nine nuclear-armed states are modernizing their arsenals, boosting their destructive capabilities. China’s nuclear arsenal is estimated to have increased from 200 to 300 warheads in the late 2010s to 620 this year. North Korea has also expanded its arsenal from an estimated ten to 20 warheads in 2018 to around 60 this year, and it has developed increasingly sophisticated launch platforms. In March, France revealed the first increase in its nuclear warhead stockpile since 1992. The United States and Russia, the world’s two largest nuclear powers, have failed to preserve the last remaining treaty constraining their strategic arsenals. And a growing number of nonnuclear powers have started to consider acquiring arsenals of their own.

    Recent findings suggest that simultaneously, artificial intelligence is powering ever more dangerous weapons of war. Human oversight is being progressively reduced as AI makes it possible to automate cyberattacks against power grids, hospitals, and financial systems. AI systems have hacked government bodies and enabled the mass production of deepfakes and disinformation campaigns.

    Recent findings suggest that the integration of AI into nuclear technologies poses an existential threat: as AI speeds up decision-making, it reduces the time available for human judgment. Similarly, the use of AI in biotechnology could dramatically lower barriers to harmful experimentation and the development of bioweapons. In both areas, this technology is elevating the risk of miscalculation, unintended escalation, and mass destruction to a level higher than ever before.

    According to recent reports, together, these dynamics are multiplying the chances that any crisis will rapidly spiral into planetary annihilation. Countries are building the instruments of catastrophe at the blinding speed of innovation while the instruments of control move at the much slower pace of diplomacy.

    It has been revealed that political change is pushing the world away from peace and toward confrontation and militarization. A multipolar world is not, by definition, a more dangerous one, but the erosion of rules and institutions that manage tensions between poles has made today’s world particularly volatile. Competition among great powers is increasing, with hegemonic ambitions encouraging assertive foreign policies and revisionist states challenging established rules and borders. Belligerent nationalism is on the rise, and far-right movements are advancing a worldview in which international relations is a zero-sum game and countries must compete rather than cooperate. Even centrist leaders are embracing the language of war preparedness. Although they do not intend to start a war, their words feed a dangerous militaristic mindset.

    In this context of rivalry, wars of aggression come wrapped in narratives of necessity, liberation, self-defense, or historical justice. The attackers present their operations as inevitable, having demonized their targets to justify preemptive action against them. They describe each war as an answer to insecurity—a war to end all wars.

    According to recent reports, but these wars will not make a safer world. Every time a state embarks on a war of aggression, it erodes the norms that protect all countries from the arbitrary use of force—including the aggressor itself.

    Wars exact immense costs. They shatter societies and interrupt lives. In 2025, at least one civilian died in an armed conflict every 14 minutes, according to UN records, and more than five million people were forced to flee their countries. The economic costs are high, too; the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran has severely disrupted maritime trade and air traffic, driving up the prices of energy, fertilizer, and other commodities, and millions of people across the world are suffering the consequences.

    Industry observers note that war also creates upcoming dangers. Once the fighting begins, its course is unpredictable. Conflict tends to draw in new actors and spill into neighboring countries. The war in Iran serves, again, as a prime example. Since February 2026, Iran has struck targets in several Gulf countries and other neighbors—actions Spain has consistently condemned. Attacks on civilian and commercial vessels threaten broader regional stability. And the war has reignited conflicts in Iraq, Lebanon, and Yemen.

    Industry observers note that finally, wars rarely produce lasting peace. Instead, they deepen grievances and entrench divisions that fuel future violence. Russia’s war in Ukraine, for instance, has destroyed trust in Moscow. The genocide in Gaza has inflamed anger toward Israel, potentially leading to fresh waves of terrorism. And the war against Iran has further destabilized the Middle East, hindering cooperation across the region.

    The world has a responsibility to resist the normalization of wars. Remaining silent is an act of cowardice and complicity. Spanish society is making its position clear: three of four Spaniards identify war as their greatest fear, and an even greater number believe another world war is on the horizon.

    But it is not enough to simply condemn war in principle. The ambition of ending war must be matched with action that makes it increasingly difficult for countries to start, sustain, and justify armed conflict.

    Spain has endeavored to take such action. It has defended the international laws that stand between an order governed by rules and one governed by force. Spain has consistently denounced armed attacks that violate the UN Charter.

    From day one of the war in Gaza, Spain has been calling for an immediate and permanent cease-fire, the release of all hostages, and the unrestricted delivery of humanitarian assistance. In May 2024, Spain recognized the state of Palestine in the hope that this step would help advance a negotiated and lasting solution to the conflict. And Spain has actively supported the efforts of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court to hold Israeli leaders accountable for violations of international humanitarian law. Israel had the right to self-defense after the October 7 terrorist attacks, but that right does not justify genocide in Gaza or the expansion of Israel’s illegal occupation of the West Bank.

    Industry observers note that deterring war also requires raising the costs of aggression. The rest of the world must ensure that those who choose to wage war cannot do so without paying a price. Throughout Russia’s war in Ukraine, for example, the European Union has introduced a series of sanctions on Russia, which Spain has consistently supported. Spain has also provided financial, humanitarian, and military assistance to Ukraine, helping it defend its territory and deny Russia the spoils of war.

    It has been revealed that countries must refuse to help belligerents expand existing conflicts. Spain, for instance, has maintained an arms embargo on Israel since 2023. This year, it also denied the United States the use of its territory and facilities for the war against Iran. Spain’s decision was not an act of hostility toward an ally. Nor was it an expression of neutrality or sympathy for the Iranian regime. It was, rather, a judgment that getting involved would enable escalation of the conflict, deepening regional and global insecurity. To keep its commitment to peace, Spain had to be willing to say no, even when doing so carried a political cost. Had more countries done the same, the wars in Gaza and Iran would have been far harder and costlier to wage.

    It has been revealed that investing in prosperity is also essential. Security is strengthened when societies are resilient, inequalities are reduced, and citizens can rely on public institutions. Spain’s decision last year to opt out of NATO’s proposed defense spending target of five percent of GDP reflected this understanding. This position did not stem from a lack of commitment to European defense—in fact, my government has championed Europe’s push for strategic autonomy and has tripled net defense spending over the eight years I have been in office. But military deterrence and social welfare must reinforce each other. By keeping defense spending proportionate, Spain has preserved the fiscal space to invest an additional 145 billion euros in social protection, housing, health care, and education, as well as more than 30 billion euros in the green transition—programs that make society more cohesive and adaptable, and therefore more secure.

    Yet one country’s efforts can accomplish only so much. Starving war of its lifelines requires all hands on deck, a collective effort rooted in genuine multilateralism. This is the only strategy that has worked before. The multilateral system built after World War II spanned the globe, and it helped keep peace among great powers and prevent a third world war.

    In a recent development, reinforcing it will not be an easy task. Geopolitical competition and widespread mistrust have weakened the United Nations, international financial bodies, regional organizations, and other multilateral institutions. Many countries perceive them as ineffective and trapped in perpetual crisis, so they have turned to alternative frameworks to try to end wars.

    Some have tried unilateral approaches, pursuing transactional bargains that end up benefiting economic and political elites while sidelining the populations affected by the conflict. The cease-fires or peace deals they achieve may be preferable to continued war, but any peace imposed through power politics rather than law rests on shaky foundations.

    According to recent reports, other countries, frustrated with multilateralism, have tried recruiting coalitions of the willing, or other “minilateral” groups, to provide security guarantees or reach ad hoc arrangements on matters of trade and technology. This approach might be a temporary solution to the paralysis of traditional institutions, but its exclusivity further fragments an already divided international order. What is needed is not minilateralism but maxilateralism. International cooperation is powerful when it is, or aspires to be, universal. Leaving part of the world outside of multilateral efforts, moreover, is a recipe for confrontation down the road.

    The twentieth-century system was not perfect. The application of its rules has been uneven, its standards inconsistently upheld, its procedures frustratingly slow. But it is undeniable that the world would be much more dangerous without it. To take just one example, it was a lattice of international treaties—including the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, and the Limited Test Ban Treaty—that ended a wildly expensive arms race that was driving the world to the brink of nuclear war.

    All of this institutional architecture is now eroding. Yet without it, the world cannot aspire to preserve peace.

    Strengthening multilateral institutions must be at the center of a global campaign to relegate war to history. This will require substantial reform to restore these institutions’ legitimacy and their capacity to act, prioritizing measures that will contribute the most to peace and security.

    Sources indicate that the first is increasing representation at the United Nations and the Bretton Woods institutions. An upgrade to the structure of the UN Security Council is particularly important, given that body’s primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace. A Security Council that gives permanent seats and a right to veto only to the five victors of World War II, which together account for barely a quarter of the global population, does not reflect today’s world. The council’s elected membership should be expanded and the terms of those members should be extended beyond the current two years. The new seats should be given primarily to countries in underrepresented regions, particularly Africa and Latin America. Regional organizations such as the European Union and the African Union should also be represented in the council, potentially taking over seats currently occupied by states. A more representative Security Council would not merely be fairer; it would also be more effective. Countries are more likely to defend and enforce international rules when they consider themselves to be authors of those rules.

    Recent findings suggest that permanent members’ veto power must also be strictly limited, particularly when the Security Council considers cases of mass atrocities, genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes. Ultimately, the veto should be abolished outright. Only then can the council respond to all acts of aggression without being paralyzed by the objections of a single state.

    A similar spirit should guide structural change at international financial institutions, particularly the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. The distribution of voting power in both still reflects twentieth-century economic balances, and by convention, a European always leads the IMF and an American leads the World Bank. This must end. Emerging economies need better representation, and leadership positions should be open to all candidates regardless of nationality. Responsibilities within institutions such as the World Trade Organization should also evolve as economic growth moves countries that were once categorized as “developing” into the ranks of the wealthy. Fairer economic governance would ease the inequality and resentment that so often feed instability and conflict.

    According to recent reports, another key reform will involve reinvigorating the international framework that limits the risk of nuclear escalation. Some of that work depends on the nuclear powers; it is up to the United States and Russia, for example, to negotiate a successor to the bilateral New START treaty that preserves verifiable limits on strategic nuclear deployments. And this time, China should be part of the discussions.

    Yet the broader effort requires the engagement of all countries. Their priorities should include ratifying the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty to prevent a resumption of nuclear testing and advancing negotiations on a Fissile Material Cutoff Treaty, which would ban production of highly enriched uranium and plutonium for nuclear weapons. All countries must also work together to regulate the use of AI in the military domain, especially when it comes to nuclear weapons, to preserve human control over launch decisions and reduce the risk of catastrophic errors. Nonnuclear powers should commit to not acquiring nuclear weapons themselves, and they should use every tool at their disposal to encourage nuclear powers to reduce their arsenals, strengthen verification mechanisms, and rebuild the diplomatic guardrails that for decades have helped prevent nuclear catastrophe.

    Recent findings suggest that technology can help with some of this. Advances in satellite imagery, remote sensors, and data analytics can increase transparency and make compliance with arms control agreements more observable. But more must be done to avoid situations that can escalate into war. If nuclear-armed states agree to lower operational readiness and strengthen crisis communication, that can help ensure that governments have the time and the means to defuse dangerous situations. Each country must protect its command-and-control systems from cyberattacks and AI-driven manipulation of information, so that a false alarm or miscalculation never leads to nuclear war.

    Recent findings suggest that the final priority is to ensure that the international justice system can enforce courts’ decisions. Dismantling the International Criminal Court, as some countries are trying to do, would only ensure that the world’s gravest crimes go unpunished. The ICC should not only prosecute cases of genocide, aggression, war crimes, and crimes against humanity but also have the authority to bring to justice those who are responsible for these crimes. When a state becomes a party to the Rome Statute, the treaty that created the ICC, it agrees to submit itself to the court’s jurisdiction. Yet if that state refuses to cooperate or surrender a suspect, there is no real punishment, only an embarrassing censure. This must change. States that shelter individuals indicted by the ICC should face legal, diplomatic, and financial consequences. Starting and waging war should carry a real cost.

    It has been revealed that proposals to reform international institutions have long struggled to gain traction, but the coming election of a new UN secretary-general offers a rare opportunity to inject fresh momentum into these efforts. Were the UN to appoint its first female leader, it would be a powerful symbol of renewal, inclusion, and institutional adaptation. The organization cannot truly claim to speak on behalf of all humanity until it has had a woman leading it. Reaching this milestone could kindle a new sense of ambition and instill greater confidence in the capacity of international institutions to reform themselves—and to reclaim their role in constraining war.

    Halting the world’s march toward war will require the broadest possible commitment. All countries, large and small, must refuse to look away or to participate in escalatory action. They must stand by the international norms that constrain war today, and reform and empower the institutions that will make it impossible tomorrow.

    Ultimately, what will make war unimaginable is a positive peace agenda that addresses the root causes of insecurity. Every step toward eradicating poverty, expanding access to quality education, advancing gender equality, strengthening democratic institutions, and increasing disaster resilience also eases the conditions that produce violence.

    Sources indicate that international financial institutions must be able to deliver financing promptly, at scale, and at reasonable cost, so that no developing country is forced to choose between servicing its debt and investing in its people. Multilateral development banks must be able to mobilize funds for the green and digital transitions, so that climate migration and competition over resources do not become drivers of interstate conflict. And the World Health Organization’s Pandemic Agreement must be finalized and put into force to ensure that all countries will be able to access vaccines and treatments when the next global health emergency strikes.

    This is why Spain has sought to place development at the heart of its foreign policy. The Spanish government has championed the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals for 2030, and last year the city of Seville hosted the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, where delegates committed to easing the debt burden of vulnerable countries and unlocking investment for sustainable development. Spain has also promoted initiatives such as the Global Hub on Debt for Development Swaps, debuted with the World Bank; the multilateral Debt Suspension Clause Alliance, which allows vulnerable countries to pause debt payments after disasters; and its own mechanism to provide up to 60 million euros in debt relief for developing countries each year. In addition, Spain has backed climate finance, global health, gender equality, food security, and social protection initiatives in partnership with multilateral institutions and international organizations. These development policies are peacebuilding policies, too.

    A larger project to rally the world behind legal norms and genuine multilateralism may seem unrealistic. But we have seen what happens when the normalization of war drags humanity into hell. The men and women who emerged from the ruins of World War II, the darkest chapter in human history, found a way to construct a multilateral world order. The question before our generation is whether we will preserve the rule of law or allow a return to rule by force. Whether we build the world of tomorrow through foresight and cooperation, or through the chaos and pain of another world war. We must choose wisely while the choice is still ours to make.

    #122611. What Did Xi Jinping Get From the Shenzhen Summit?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1580 w)

    What Did Xi Jinping Get From the Shenzhen Summit?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1580 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A brief summit between the leaders of China, the United States, and Russia was held in Shenzhen, China, on Nov.
    • Sources indicate that in my view, the summit, short as it was, did matter.
    • In a recent development, A brief summit between the leaders of China, the United States, and Russia was held in Shenzhen, China, on Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    A brief summit between the leaders of China, the United States, and Russia was held in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19. Critics saw little substantive achievement, arguing that the three had merely taken advantage of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum to meet for a photo opportunity. Some American observers faulted U.S. President Donald Trump in particular for yielding to China and Russia rather than showing leadership.

    Sources indicate that in my view, the summit, short as it was, did matter. In great-power politics, the format can sometimes matter more than the concrete results. The leaders of the three countries had never sat down together in this format; that they managed to do so notes something about the kind of era that we are entering.

    In a recent development, A brief summit between the leaders of China, the United States, and Russia was held in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19. Critics saw little substantive achievement, arguing that the three had merely taken advantage of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum to meet for a photo opportunity. Some American observers faulted U.S. President Donald Trump in particular for yielding to China and Russia rather than showing leadership.

    Sources indicate that in my view, the summit, short as it was, did matter. In great-power politics, the format can sometimes matter more than the concrete results. The leaders of the three countries had never sat down together in this format; that they managed to do so indicates something about the kind of era that we are entering.

    Recent findings suggest that in an era of great-power politics, one of the keys to avoiding military conflict is for the powers to hear one another out. They did so in Shenzhen. They also exceeded expectations by issuing a joint peace declaration with four points of agreement. And for Chinese President Xi Jinping in particular, the summit offered a first chance to try out an approach to great-power relations that he had originally proposed to Washington, this time with both the United States and Russia at the table.

    According to recent reports, yet while Xi hosted, the biggest winner was clearly Russian President Vladimir Putin. The war in Ukraine has left Russia diplomatically isolated from much of the West. Shenzhen could not end that isolation, but it revealed that Russia could not simply be shut out of great-power diplomacy. Russia is a major military power and rich in natural resources, but its overall strength still falls well short of that of the United States or China. By sitting down with Putin as an equal, the Chinese and American leaders acknowledged that Russia remains a power that they cannot bypass on questions of global strategic security.

    Industry observers note that xi was a winner, too. Beijing showed that it could bring two adversaries, the United States and Russia, together on Chinese soil and secure a joint declaration. The format itself put China back at the center of the international stage. A decade ago, it would have been hard to imagine China convening such a meeting. That also helped Xi’s standing at home.

    In a recent development, trump had just suffered a crushing defeat in the midterm elections. Yet both China and Russia accorded him the respect due an American president with whom they could still discuss strategic matters. China, in particular, gave him a lavish welcome rather than treating him as a lame duck.

    Recent findings suggest that but the three leaders did not sit around a table simply for the sake of appearances, and Xi in particular made some meaningful gains here. The Chinese president raised the question of how the three powers should deal with one another from here on. His answer: with mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, mutually beneficial cooperation, and dialogue and consultation.

    Industry observers note that these are principles that Beijing has long pressed in its dealings with Washington, rooted in Xi’s proposal for a “upcoming type of great-power relations” between China and the United States. As host, Xi set the tone by extending that framework to all three countries. The summit was a chance for Beijing to put it into practice. In effect, Xi brought Putin into the room to press Trump on an approach that he had long advocated for U.S.-China relations.

    That, from Beijing’s perspective, was the summit’s most important achievement. Rivalry between Washington and Beijing, and outright hostility between Washington and Moscow, did not prevent the three countries from coordinating on strategic stability.

    This takes a minimum of trust. None of the three countries has to believe that its rivals will give up competing. Each has to believe that the others also want to prevent a miscalculation from triggering a conflict, that they are willing to explain their intentions, and that they will listen when another country spells out its red lines. Sitting down together, rather than meeting only in pairs, means letting down their guard enough to acknowledge that some risks involve all three and cannot necessarily be managed through bilateral talks alone.

    Sources indicate that if regular coordination takes hold, then Shenzhen will matter even more to Beijing. After the summit, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi remarked that China would stay in touch with Russia and the United States at the working level. That is a start. Whether the leaders’ dialogue lasts will depend on whether they meet a second or third time, and whether communication holds up when relations come under strain.

    Those gains stem largely from the format. The declaration itself offers further clues to what Beijing wanted to accomplish. The first, third, and fourth points are particularly revealing.

    The first concerns U.N. reform. The three countries agreed to work toward reforming the United Nations so it could respond more effectively to global challenges and better fulfill its basic mission of maintaining international peace and security.

    My reading is that Beijing pushed for this language to reassure the global south. Beijing knows that some countries in the global south are uneasy about China sitting down with the United States and Russia at a summit of its own making. Putting the U.N. reform first sent a related message: The three powers had met to help the United Nations fulfill its peace and security mandate and had no intention of making fresh rules over the heads of the global south. Wang’s insistence after the summit that countries large and small are equal was meant to convey the same point.

    According to recent reports, the third point in the declaration names the International Criminal Court. The leaders emphasized the importance of state consent and respect for the immunity of state officials, and they stated the court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction. Moscow likely pushed for this provision in response to the court’s arrest warrant for Putin, backed by Trump due to the U.S. far right’s hostility toward the court. But the words “and other similar bodies” were most likely added at Beijing’s insistence. They give China a joint statement that it can cite in future disputes over jurisdiction, such as the South China Sea arbitration.

    Those words also have implications for Taiwan. If mainland China were to attack Taiwan and Washington were to push for Chinese leaders to be held criminally accountable for alleged war crimes, Beijing could point to a declaration the United States helped concern and ask: What did you say in Shenzhen about state consent and the immunity of officials?

    Recent findings suggest that the fourth point can be read as a gain for Beijing on nuclear issues. The three countries reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought—language that originated with U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, but that has been taken up by China. They also agreed to hold talks on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation.

    Industry observers note that trump wanted trilateral nuclear disarmament talks. What made it into the declaration was language on risk reduction and nonproliferation. Beijing succeeded in redirecting U.S. pressure to join disarmament talks toward concerns that all three countries might be willing to keep discussing.

    Industry observers note that china also gained a basis for putting diplomatic pressure on Japan, where changes to—or even the abandonment of—the three non-nuclear principles are under consideration. If Tokyo goes down that path, particularly if the debate turns to Japan acquiring nuclear weapons of its own, Beijing can cite the trilateral agreement and press Washington to say where it stands on those risks.

    Industry observers note that xi demonstrated at Shenzhen that China could convene two adversaries, set a framework for discussing strategic stability, and get them to agree on some common positions. As much criticism as the meeting drew, it also raised hopes that trilateral talks might become a regular fixture. Xi’s remarks suggest that he would like to see that happen. The real test will come when the three countries face a crisis and their interests collide. Will they still be willing to talk the way that they did in Shenzhen?

    Deng Yuwen is a Chinese writer and scholar.

    #122608. China Doesn’t Want a Nuclear Arms Race

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2816 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    China Doesn’t Want a Nuclear Arms Race

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2816 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • GOLDSTEIN is Director of the Asia Program at Defense Priorities and Director of the China Initiative at Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs.
    • NINA TANNENWALD is Associate Teaching Professor of Political Science at Brown University.
    • Recent findings suggest that today, pessimism—almost fatalism—reigns in Washington about the United States’ ability to avoid a costly and dangerous arms race with China.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that LYLE J. GOLDSTEIN is Director of the Asia Program at Defense Priorities and Director of the China Initiative at Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs.

    NINA TANNENWALD is Associate Teaching Professor of Political Science at Brown University.

    How America Can Avert an Unnecessary Rivalry.

    Lyle J. Goldstein and Nina Tannenwald.

    Recent findings suggest that today, pessimism—almost fatalism—reigns in Washington about the United States’ ability to avoid a costly and dangerous arms race with China. Policymakers point to China’s increasingly aggressive policies toward Taiwan, its massive military buildup, and its resistance to engaging in some arms control measures as evidence that Beijing has accepted the inevitability of such a race or is even pursuing one. Worried by intellectual frameworks that emphasize the likelihood of war between rival great powers, many U.S. leaders and analysts see little choice but for the United States to arm itself, too. But this thinking risks becoming a self-fulling prophecy. The major danger is that an unrestrained arms race increases the likelihood of war over Taiwan or even of a catastrophic nuclear exchange.

    Sources indicate that but the pessimism about averting an arms race is misplaced. A nuclear arms race, in particular, is not a foregone conclusion—and the United States has real opportunities to curb one. Avoiding a nuclear arms race will require a broader approach than the two-pronged one Washington has recently favored: building up U.S. nuclear deterrence and seeking to force concessions from Beijing by imposing restrictions on trade and technology transfers. American leaders should instead look beyond traditional deterrence, which falls short because its threat-based approach tends to provoke competition over arms, and strive to establish a more fundamental strategic stability through a process of reciprocal de-escalation and compromise. China is likely to be amenable to reciprocal de-escalation: it has a long tradition of moderation in nuclear matters and, ultimately, Chinese leaders do not want a war over Taiwan.

    It has been revealed that there are recent signs that even U.S. President Donald Trump, who has often boasted about his distaste for compromise, sees the value of engagement. After two U.S.-Chinese bilateral summits this year, in October he suggested that his November trilateral meeting in Shenzhen with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin should focus on “denuclearization.” But Washington will have to become much more consistent in its rejection of an arms race, including by modifying its support for Taiwan and incorporating China into global arms control leadership. A nuclear arms race with China becomes inevitable only if Washington continues to believe it is.

    China is undoubtedly pursuing a military buildup, including investments in nuclear weapons. Between 2020 and 2025, China doubled the number of its nuclear warheads, from 300 to 600—a startling increase, although its arsenal remains small compared with the United States’ approximately 3,700 warheads. In 2021, researchers at the Federation of American Scientists confirmed that China was constructing 350 upcoming nuclear missile silos in three vast sites in Xinjiang and Gansu provinces. Beijing is also pursuing substantial qualitative upgrades to its nuclear weapons, a push it showcased at an October 2025 military parade that unveiled a new sea-released ballistic missile, two new kinds of intercontinental ballistic missiles, a new air-launched hypersonic missile, and a new long-range hypersonic cruise missile.

    It has been revealed that then, this July, the Chinese navy tested a submarine-rolled out long-range ballistic missile that could carry nuclear weapons. This significant new capability will allow China to launch long-range nuclear strikes that can reach the United States from protected waters near its own coastline rather than having to sail out into the Pacific. A recent editorial in a leading Chinese foreign affairs newspaper took the candid yet disturbing step of explicitly linking China’s rapid nuclear buildup to its desire to exert sovereignty over Taiwan. “The great cause of national reunification,” it asserted, “must rest on a solid, realistic foundation. That foundation is, first and foremost, hard power.” Although such overt nuclear saber rattling remains rare, the link between Beijing’s nuclear forces and the Taiwan glitch stretches back over three decades and is also supported by the scholar Tong Zhao’s detailed analysis of China’s nuclear buildup in Foreign Affairs in May.

    As China builds up its military, the perception that it is on a collision course with the United States over Taiwan—one that inevitably includes the risk of nuclear escalation—has become widespread in Washington. Taiwan, of course, appears to be an obvious flash point. The United States has long committed itself informally to defending the island while China seeks to unify with it, by force if necessary. In October, Army General Ronald Clark, the head of the U.S. Pacific Command, affirmed that his forces are actively readying for a Chinese invasion of Taiwan that could come as early as 2027.

    The Biden administration and both Trump administrations made some attempts to engage China over arms control and nuclear risk reduction. Trump proposed trilateral arms control talks that would include Russia, whereas the Biden administration pursued bilateral talks with China on strategic stability and nuclear risk reduction. But both presidents gave up after China consistently rejected engaging in sustained talks on nuclear matters. Beijing’s stance is that it has a small nuclear arsenal compared with the United States and Russia and that it is vital to first establish trust and mutual reassurance about core interests.

    Industry observers note that beyond China’s resistance to arms control, theories about power that are trendy in Washington reinforce the collision course mentality. Numerous realist scholars argue that a U.S.-Chinese rivalry and even a great-power war may be structurally difficult to avoid. The political scientist Graham Allison captured this pessimism in his influential 2017 book, Destined for War, which argued that a so-called Thucydides trap—when a rapidly rising power challenges the position of the dominant power, yielding war—would doom the United States and China to conflict.

    Recent findings suggest that china hawks, such as Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby, increasingly advocate an aggressive focus on “preparing for World War III” with China as a way to avoid it. In a July Latest York Times interview, Colby argued that the United States must “deny” China “the ability to seize and hold the key territory” of Taiwan, by enhancing U.S. deterrence with a massive military buildup. The next month, speaking at a military conference, Colby specified that such a buildup ought to put a greater emphasis on tactical nuclear weapons and the ability to fight a so-called limited nuclear war. The enemy, Colby said, has “got to believe there’s some sense in which we would use” nuclear weapons. Toward this end, the United States is building a new intercontinental ballistic missile, a new air-launched cruise missile, and new nuclear-armed submarines and bombers, and accelerating the ambitious Golden Dome homeland missile defense project. Unlike earlier U.S. missile defenses, which were designed to intercept limited strikes by so called rogue states such as Iran and North Korea, the Golden Dome is intended to defend against massive Chinese or Russian attacks. But the prospect of losing its ability to retaliate against a U.S. first strike only gives Beijing more incentive to expand its nuclear arsenal.

    It has been revealed that such a nuclear-heavy approach only prevents a war with China if nuclear deterrence succeeds. That puts a lot of eggs in the deterrence basket. And recent wars suggest that nuclear deterrence is becoming less effective. Russia’s nuclear threats have not coerced Ukraine into halting its strikes deep into Russian territory. Iran has proved willing to launch strikes against nuclear-armed Israel as well as U.S. bases and allies in the Middle East. What is most ominous, in May 2025, India and Pakistan crossed previous redlines and attacked each other’s homelands, something that mutual nuclear deterrence was supposed to prevent. Even if neither the United States nor China want nuclear war, a China determined to unify with Taiwan may not be intimidated by U.S. nuclear threats.

    Recent findings suggest that A recent study by Brown University’s Costs of War program found that the United States has already spent more than $3.4 trillion on its militarized rivalry with China over the last decade. Sustaining or ramping up this spending—which encompasses new warships, aircraft, long-range missiles, drones, base upgrades, forward deployments, large military exercises, research and development, and new nuclear weapons—is infeasible in an era of ballooning national debt and expanding domestic needs.

    Recent findings suggest that one of the tragedies of an arms race is that neither party may actually want to pursue one. Despite its current arms buildup, Beijing has a long record of moderation in military and nuclear matters. For many decades, it has maintained a minimal nuclear deterrent and a no-first-use policy, and it did not use major military force to achieve strategic goals. Although it has long had access to the relevant technologies, China appears not to have produced or deployed tactical nuclear weapons. Chinese diplomats played a substantial role in coaxing Iran to accept the Obama administration’s 2015 nuclear deal and supported the UN’s relatively stringent sanctions on North Korea. And in the fall of 2022, according to then Secretary of State Antony Blinken and reporting by the Financial Times, China likely intervened diplomatically with the Kremlin to help stop Russia from using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. More broadly, China has embraced international law when it comes to war, playing a constructive role, for example, in removing chemical weapons from Syria in 2013.

    Industry observers note that beijing’s inclination toward restraint has not disappeared completely, even as it upgrades its military. In November 2023, U.S. President Joe Biden and Xi agreed to renew lines of communication between their countries’ militaries that had been severed after U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taiwan the previous year. A year later, the two leaders affirmed that humans, not AI, must control the decision to use nuclear weapons. And in late 2025, Beijing released a white paper emphatically reiterating its support for nuclear arms control and has moved toward more transparency by publishing more information, including in English, about its military upgrades.

    Chinese leaders clearly do not want a war over Taiwan. Publicly, they repeatedly emphasize that their goal is “peaceful unification” and “winning without fighting,” invoking the Chinese strategist Sun-tzu. Beijing’s longtime “one country, two systems” policy toward Taiwan—which would bring the island under Chinese sovereignty while allowing it substantial autonomy—leaves room for a negotiated solution. Last year, in an notable analysis of China’s strategic ambitions, the scholars David Kang, Jackie Wong, and Zenobia Chan examined 12,000 articles and hundreds of speeches by Xi to argue that Beijing prioritizes regime stability and internal development over displacing the United States as a global military hegemon. Although China’s major, unannounced exercises around Taiwan earlier this month may constitute an exception, overall, Chinese military exercises near Taiwan over the last five years are consistent with this interpretation: many have reacted to perceived provocations, illustrate only medium-scale capabilities, and have generally had a performative quality, accompanied by extensive press coverage.

    There is still an opening for the United States and China to de-escalate. To achieve strategic stability, the two countries will need to make a concerted effort to defuse their security dilemma—the dynamic in which each side perceives the other’s defensive measures as aggressive. First, U.S. and Chinese leaders need to revive superpower summitry. Biden held only three face-to-face meetings with Xi on the sidelines of regional economic meetings. Although the May 2026 Beijing summit between Trump and Xi yielded no major breakthroughs, the meeting did improve the two leaders’ personal relationship; today, U.S.-Chinese tensions are lower than they were between 2021 and 2025. This progress suggests the great value of holding a regular, annual, multiday bilateral summit with a significant focus on nuclear arms control. Such meetings would give expert working groups time to methodically develop measures to reduce the risk of conflict. Just as crucial, the summits need to be long enough to leave room for unscripted conversations. At their first summit, in Geneva in November 1985, U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev famously broke away from anxious bureaucrats and advisers for an impromptu walk—an encounter that helped establish a more constructive relationship.

    According to recent reports, the United States must also take concrete steps to reduce the chance of escalation in the Taiwan Strait. Above all, it should adhere more consistently to its “one China” policy—its position that Beijing is the sole legal government of China. More consistency would include limiting U.S. legislators’ trips to the island and downgrading U.S.-Taiwanese defense relations by, for example, holding meetings less frequently and at lower diplomatic levels. Washington should remind key allies such as Japan to proceed cautiously in terms of their rhetoric and military deployments. Such a restraint-oriented strategy would make it clear to Taiwan that independence is off the table, encouraging it to take a more accommodating approach that would lower the temperature with Beijing. If Washington were to agree to common-sense limitations on arms sales to Taiwan—such as refusing to sell Taiwan the surface-to-surface ballistic Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS), which can reach across the strait to the Chinese mainland—Beijing would likely reciprocate by scaling back its military exercises and related military deployments around the island. There are real incentives for Beijing to de-escalate. Doing so could improve relations with neighbors such as Japan, free up focus for domestic priorities, lower military spending, and limit the chance of war.

    According to recent reports, the Pentagon needs to demonstrate Washington’s intent to avoid war over Taiwan by gradually decreasing U.S. warship transits through the Taiwan Strait. Even more notable, Washington should also substantially reduce U.S. military deployments in the Luzon Strait between Taiwan and the Philippines and around Japan’s Ryukyu Islands. Such deployments only exacerbate the security dilemma.

    According to recent reports, exhibiting restraint does not mean the United States would be giving Taiwan away. The United States can continue to provide Taiwan with defensive arms (such as missile interceptors, artillery, drones, and mines) and harden U.S. bases in the region to provide stabilizing deterrence. But even if U.S. leaders publicly abjure direct military intervention to defend Taiwan—a rational step that would lower the risk of nuclear war—China will prefer negotiating with Taipei on the island’s autonomy over a bloody military showdown with Taiwanese forces. For their part, Taiwan’s leaders will likely accommodate themselves to limited self-governance under Chinese overall sovereignty. In the end, China’s main goal is to get Taiwan out of the U.S. sphere of influence. Chinese leaders’ major fear is not so much Taiwanese autonomy as the prospect of the island serving as a U.S. forward base—in Chinese parlance, “using Taiwan to contain China.”.

    Sources indicate that another important step would be to seek a multilateral pledge by all nuclear-armed states to employ nuclear weapons only in retaliation against a nuclear attack. Such a policy would reduce the risk of miscalculation during a crisis. China has long embraced such a no-first-use policy, but U.S. leaders have traditionally opposed it, believing that it might expose U.S. allies to conventional attack. The U.S. nuclear deterrent for allies, however, increasingly lacks credibility because the costs of starting a nuclear war would vastly outweigh the benefits. And after the collapse of traditional nuclear arms control, a mutual no-first-use policy offers a promising area of common ground between the United States and China. It would reinforce the existing no-first-use policies of China and India and implicitly acknowledge their leadership in the area of nuclear restraint, a virtue when newer nuclear states are chafing under the old Cold War superpowers’ dominance of arms control. This approach could even entice Beijing into a wider, more comprehensive process of bilateral or multilateral nuclear arms control.

    Beyond these three major initiatives, the United States and China should sign an agreement to notify each other about their ballistic missile tests. Washington could also consider giving Beijing a larger role in nonproliferation efforts, for instance by affording China leadership roles in negotiations and inspection regimes in future nonproliferation arrangements. The U.S. arms control agenda with China should focus not only on offensive nuclear systems but also on missile defenses and tactical nuclear weapons, as well as AI technologies. And it would help if the United States evolved its own nuclear posture in the direction of restraint by reducing its warheads, warfighting capabilities, and alert posture.

    Sources indicate that ultimately, the United States needs to get serious about reining in an arms race with China before its perception that one is apace becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. The two countries have a mutual interest in restraint. If Washington continues to overlook Beijing’s incentives to compromise—and the real signs that it is willing to do so—an arms race that, as of now, is mostly putative will become a reality. And a catastrophic war that could have been avoided could indeed become inevitable.

    #122606. Tech Giants Are Effectively Ungovernable. Here’s How to Change That.
