    Tech Giants Are Effectively Ungovernable. Here’s How to Change That.

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2322 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that american business has minted a newly introduced brand of executive: the CEO who is too big to fire.
    • Three years earlier, OpenAI’s board had dismissed Sam Altman, citing a lack of candor with directors.
    • American business has minted a newly introduced brand of executive: the CEO who is too substantial to fire.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    It has been revealed that american business has minted a newly introduced brand of executive: the CEO who is too big to fire. On Nov. 17, Nvidia’s board declared that it had accepted the resignation of Jensen Huang, felled by an affair with an alleged Chinese spy and a romance with one of the executive’s own subordinates. Six days later, Huang was back, restored after a unanimous vote by the same board. Nvidia’s shares soared. Many investors celebrated the return of the leather-jacketed founder credited with making the company the engine of the artificial intelligence revolution.

    Three years earlier, OpenAI’s board had dismissed Sam Altman, citing a lack of candor with directors. Five days later, Altman returned, and most of the directors responsible for his removal were out.

    American business has minted a newly introduced brand of executive: the CEO who is too substantial to fire. On Nov. 17, Nvidia’s board declared that it had accepted the resignation of Jensen Huang, felled by an affair with an alleged Chinese spy and a romance with one of the executive’s own subordinates. Six days later, Huang was back, restored after a unanimous vote by the same board. Nvidia’s shares soared. Many investors celebrated the return of the leather-jacketed founder credited with making the company the engine of the artificial intelligence revolution.

    It has been revealed that three years earlier, OpenAI’s board had dismissed Sam Altman, citing a lack of candor with directors. Five days later, Altman returned, and most of the directors responsible for his removal were out.

    In both cases, directors discovered that formal authority to remove a chief executive does not mean the power to do so in practice. The episodes exposed a three-pronged weakness in corporate governance: the challenge of maverick founders, the extraordinary complexity of AI, and the growing dependence of the U.S. economy and national security on a handful of companies at the technological frontier.

    In a recent development, both Altman and Huang have personas, know-how, and market-moving power that made them unfireable. Yet if the boards of the country’s most consequential technology firms cannot exercise ultimate authority over management, these companies are effectively ungovernable. This reveals a major gap in corporate stewardship, underscoring the imperative of robust regulation to ensure that the vulnerabilities of powerful U.S. companies do not become fatal weaknesses for the country’s democracy and society writ large.

    The iconic corporate founder is a hallmark of U.S. business culture. Henry Ford and Andrew Carnegie shaped society-altering industries around their personalities and distinctive working styles. Steve Jobs provides the most celebrated historic example of this type of figure in tech. Forced out of Apple in 1985, Jobs returned in 1997 when the company was in steep decline. His track record of inventiveness helped win back employees, customers, investors, and developers. He also persuaded Bill Gates to invest $150 million in Apple and commit to developing Microsoft software for Macintosh computers, building an ecosystem whose fortunes were intertwined with his own and that has dominated the market for decades.

    These bold founders may have as much in common with an artist or creator than they do with fellow CEOs. A great architect or film director works with large teams but puts an unmistakable stamp on their work. Although a studio or tradition can continue after its originator dies or departs, investors, collaborators, and audiences do not always stay on.

    In a recent development, this analogy helps explain why succession at frontier technology companies is so fraught. Investors bet on a founder’s judgment about technologies whose commercial potential is unproven. Engineers are inspired by a particular visionary. Customers and business partners invest in the future that the founder promises. As these forces rally, they reify perceptions of an individual’s genius, which attracts still more talent and capital. Confidence becomes self-perpetuating.

    Such devotion is measurable. Huang topped Glassdoor’s 2026 ranking of CEOs with a 99 percent approval rating among employee reviewers. Thousands of employees reportedly signed a letter seeking his reinstatement this month. His reportedly cruel behavior toward certain employees seemingly did little to puncture that aura.

    Industry observers note that openAI’s 2023 crisis demonstrated the power of such fealty. After its board fired Altman, more than 95 percent of the organization’s employees signed a letter threatening to resign unless he came back. Microsoft, OpenAI’s largest commercial partner, rolled out a red carpet to Altman, promising to allow him to rebuild his team there. Faced with losing the workforce that was OpenAI’s principal asset, the board folded. The employees, investors, and commercial partners whose confidence had helped make Altman successful overpowered those charged with supervising him.

    Recent findings suggest that these examples do not prove that founders are irreplaceable. Apple’s revenues more than doubled during the early years of John Sculley’s post-Jobs tenure in the 1980s; more recently, the manufacturer has thrived under Tim Cook since Jobs’s death. When Uber’s Travis Kalanick was forced out in 2017, investors worried about losing the transportation innovator’s aggressive founder. His successor, Dara Khosrowshahi, now presides over a company that generated $193 billion in gross bookings and $10 billion in free cash flow in 2025.

    Board members are a little like grandparents. They admire and care about the baby, comforted that the parent—the CEO—does the daily grind. When the parent disappears, the board is left holding a crying, demanding infant. Sedate quarterly meetings suddenly turn into frantic round-the-clock Zooms. Having lost the one person who they trusted to raise the child, boards want nothing more than to once again pass the progeny into capable hands.

    Sources indicate that when it comes to AI companies, the problem is magnified by the extraordinary gap between a CEO’s knowledge of frontier technologies and what even accomplished directors can understand. Nvidia’s 10-person board includes Melissa Lora, the former president of Taco Bell; Stephen Neal, a distinguished trial lawyer; and Dawn Hudson, a former Pepsi-Cola and National Football League marketing executive. Three of the 10 have served on the board for more than 28 years each. Just one is under the age of 60. While several board members have technology backgrounds, the emergence of Nvidia’s chips and financing as lynchpins of AI competition has transformed the demands on a group of directors who were chosen at least in part because Huang trusted them not to get in his way. Alongside bleeding-edge technologies, the board is now dealing with matters of foreign espionage, regulatory capture, securities fraud, and export controls. It’s not hard to imagine Nvidia’s directors feeling out of their depth.

    The governance challenges created by Nvidia’s technological complexity are compounded by the company’s centrality to the U.S. economy and national security. A 2026 investment analysis estimated that 42 AI-related stocks accounted for 60 percent of the S&P 500’s gains in 2025. By September 2026, Nvidia alone represented approximately 8.4 percent of the index. Huang’s reinstatement on Monday propelled a broader market rally, underscoring how closely U.S. financial fortunes have become tied to confidence in the AI industry. The national-security dependence is at least as consequential. AI is increasingly incorporated into military intelligence, surveillance, cyber operations, logistics, and command-and-control systems. Access to advanced computing is at the heart of competitive tensions with China.

    In a recent development, these dependencies help explain U.S. President Donald Trump’s extraordinary intervention in Nvidia’s leadership deliberations. According to Semafor, the president called into a Nvidia board meeting to press for Huang’s return, suggesting that China might recruit him if Nvidia failed to take him back. Though no investigation has been completed and the allegations of Chinese plotting to compromise Huang are alarming, Trump personally vouched that his return would pose no national security risk. It is hard to know who possesses greater leverage in the Trump-Huang relationship—the president who controls regulatory decisions or the corporate titan whose technology is essential to domestic prosperity and national security.

    Reliance on individual technology entrepreneurs for vital national functions can compromise public interests. In October, Ukrainian forces experienced serious disruptions to Starshield satellite communications, impairing military operations. Elon Musk subsequently acknowledged that his manufacturer, SpaceX, had restricted certain uses of the service, though responsibility for the disruptions remains contested. Society depends on interconnected technological systems that are vulnerable to malfunction and compromise; the power vested in a handful of tech moguls who control these networks is staggering.

    Industry observers note that U.S. institutions have failed to reckon with this amalgamation of power. Congress remains divided over how to regulate AI. Federal agencies possess fragmented authority over specific risks and no mandate from the White House to address them. Companies develop capabilities faster than public institutions can assess them. CEOs with immense technical resources and public influence end up guiding the officials responsible for overseeing them.

    In a recent development, the consequences of this glaring void will reverberate internationally. U.S. corporate leadership is predicated on the perception that U.S. companies operate within a system of enforceable laws, strong oversight, and credible government institutions. This distinguishes U.S. technology from Chinese alternatives, whose governance remains vulnerable to direct state intervention. But if U.S. boards cannot meaningfully restrain powerful executives, and the president can intervene in their internal deliberations, those differentiators collapse. Governments considering whose AI infrastructure to trust will ask whether U.S. companies offer genuine institutional safeguards.

    The obvious response is to strengthen corporate oversight. Some mechanisms already exist. Nvidia has an independent board, audit and governance committees, and a confidential reporting hotline. It has now added a specialized national security committee and is upgrading its compliance function. OpenAI maintains a safety and security committee overseeing its operations. But all these arrangements depend on directors whose authority may be subsumed by founder loyalty, commercial pressure, and technological complexity.

    Sources indicate that other highly regulated industries offer more robust, proven oversight models. Under Federal Reserve rules, large bank holding companies must maintain independent risk committees, including directors with relevant expertise; chief risk officers report directly to those committees as well as management. Britain requires senior executives at financial firms to be approved by regulators, makes it clear what each is responsible for, and can hold them personally accountable if they fail to take reasonable steps to prevent wrongdoing. U.S. pharmaceutical regulation provides another precedent. Federal rules give drug manufacturers’ quality-control arms the authority to approve or reject products and manufacturing procedures, so that decisions do not lie simply with a CEO’s commercial preferences.

    Industry observers note that these models suggest an approach to governing companies whose technologies pose exceptional public risks. Congress should establish an independent federal supervisory authority for designated frontier AI companies, including critical infrastructure providers and developers of exceptionally capable models. Its jurisdiction should depend on the risks and systemic importance of technology companies, rather than their size or public-company status. Now that corporate interests have captured the U.S. executive branch, legislative oversight is essential.

    Such an institution would need permanent technical staff with expertise in advanced computing, model capabilities, cybersecurity, and intelligence threats. It would require secure access to proprietary information, the power to inspect governance systems, and the authority to compel corrective action. Its independence from day-to-day political intervention would be essential.

    Meanwhile, regulated companies should have dedicated board-level risk committees staffed by directors with technical and national-security competence. Those committees should retain their own expert advisors and receive regular reports from both the CEO and independent risk, safety, and compliance officers. Boards should be required to document how they evaluate consequential decisions, oversee potential conflicts of interest, and prepare for abrupt leadership transitions.

    A further priority is genuine protection for whistleblowers. Nvidia’s formal policies prohibit retaliation, yet recent reporting suggests that employees fear speaking openly. In technology companies, confidentiality is increasingly difficult to preserve. Employers can potentially reconstruct a source’s identity from records of device use, badge access, communications, and document activity, even when a reporter or investigator promises anonymity. One shudders to think what this might mean for Nvidia employees who recently spoke out about mistreatment or alleged misdeeds, believing that Huang’s tenure was over for good.

    A modern whistleblower regime should offer secure channels outside the firm, enforceable restrictions on attempts to identify confidential sources, and meaningful penalties for retaliation. An independent regulator should interview employees and business partners without requiring them to expose themselves to management. Such protections are particularly important during investigations involving a powerful founder.

    Sources indicate that it may be tempting to conclude that Nvidia’s crisis ended happily once Huang returned and the market rallied. The OpenAI episode invited a similar reaction, especially as the firm continued its rapid expansion after Altman’s reinstatement. But neither recovery resolves the institutional weakness that allowed directors’ decisions to be reversed under pressure.

    U.S. technological leadership cannot depend on a system in which the most influential executives are effectively irreplaceable. A firm that is too major to lose its founder may also be too powerful to govern itself. As AI becomes embedded in the economy, national security, and public life, the United States needs oversight institutions capable of withstanding the demands of employees, investors, politicians, and even the most celebrated innovators. The long-term credibility of U.S. technological leadership will depend on it.

    Suzanne Nossel is a columnist at Foreign Policy, the Lester Crown senior fellow for U.S. foreign policy and international order at the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, and a senior advisor to the Starling Institute. She is the author of Dare to Speak: Defending Free Speech for All. X: @SuzanneNossel.

    'RADICAL LEFT LUNATIC' JUDGE TRUMP WANTED IMPEACHED TAKES UP ILHAN OMAR WARRANT FIGHT.

    "Just a few years ago, Chief Judge Boasberg ruled that search warrant proceedings and related documents should not be made open to the public while an investigation is ongoing," the DOJ remarked in an emergency ex parte brief in opposition to the unsealing.

    According to recent reports, "The Chief Judge was merely echoing many other courts—like the D.C. Circuit, the Ninth Circuit, the Fourth Circuit, and others when he said that," the brief continued.

    The case to which the DOJ referred — where Boasberg ruled that search warrant documents should remain under seal during active investigations — was none other than Special Counsel Jack Smith's probe into Trump for alleged election interference after his 2020 presidential loss, and for the alleged retention of classified documents.

    Industry observers note that trump was indicted in both of those investigations. All the charges were eventually dropped.

    Judge James Boasberg, President Donald Trump (Valerie Plesch, Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images).

    In that case, like the Omar case, media organizations sought to unseal a warrant related to the search. Specifically, the press wanted to view a warrant obtained by Smith related to Twitter's records associated with Trump's account, @realDonaldTrump.

    Boasberg's tune was much different in that case, when, like in the Omar case, the government asked him to keep the warrant under seal due to the ongoing nature of the case.

    Notably, Trump had already been indicted when Boasberg ruled that the records needed to remain sealed while Omar has not been indicted.

    "Ultimately, the undeniable need to protect an ongoing criminal investigation tips the balance toward the Government’s request to continue sealing," Boasberg wrote in his Nov. 29, 2023 ruling.

    The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on the apparent u-turn from the judge.

    Industry observers note that rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., is denying that federal agents have told her what she is under investigation for and speaks to Fox News Digital about the status of her items that were seized after her Washington, D.C., home was raided Oct. 12, 2026.     In the Omar case, government lawyers remarked they weren't opposed to releasing the documents at an appropriate future date, but did not want them unsealed while the case is ongoing. Boasberg didn't find that argument compelling.

    But in the case against Trump, he did.

    "There may yet come a time when press access becomes appropriate, but at present the Application is a premature bid for sensitive information pertaining to an active investigation," he wrote in 2023.

    Throughout his 2023 ruling in favor of the government's bid to keep the warrant in the Trump case sealed, Boasberg continually noted the government's ability to keep warrants under seal.

    ILHAN OMAR HUDDLES WITH HER DC-BASED LAWYERS DURING HER FIRST DAY BACK ON CAPITOL HILL AMID FEDERAL PROBES.

    He stated in a second instance: "When it comes to an active investigation, the Government 'has always been able to restrict access to warrant materials by requesting a sealing order, which courts have granted freely upon a showing that a given criminal investigation requires secrecy,'" Boasberg's ruling said.

    In response to the media's claim that the First Amendment should be a deciding factor in unsealing the Trump warrant, Boasberg disagreed.

    "The historical practice is somewhat muddled, but it suggests that the First Amendment does not open search warrants and related documents to public examination when an investigation is ongoing. Search-warrant applications traditionally have been filed ex parte and thus out of the public’s view.".

    The DOJ confirmed in a brief statement to Fox News Digital on Tuesday that the characterization that Boasberg contradicted himself in unsealing the Omar documents "is accurate and a point we have made in our court filings.".

    One matter distinguishing Boasberg's ruling in the 2023 Trump case from the Omar case is the Constitution's Speech or Debate Clause, which shields lawmakers from certain government intrusions into their legislative work.

    In the Omar case, the Justice Department argued that searching her home did not involve those protections. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh disagreed and required safeguards for potentially privileged materials.

    It has been revealed that boasberg later questioned why the legal arguments over those constitutional protections should remain sealed when sensitive investigative details could be redacted.     It has been revealed that boasberg has also faced scrutiny over investigative secrecy during the Biden-era Arctic Frost probe, when he signed nondisclosure orders tied to subpoenas for Republican lawmakers' phone records.     Understanding the conflict four years in.

    Industry observers note that welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at delayed U.S. Patriot air defense missile shipments to Ukraine, Israeli forces killing a top Hamas official, and yet another purge within China’s leadership.

    Industry observers note that as Russia batters Ukraine’s cities with missile strikes, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has delayed sending scores of Patriot air defense missiles to the embattled country, including those held by European nations, according to a Financial Times report.

    Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at delayed U.S. Patriot air defense missile shipments to Ukraine, Israeli forces killing a top Hamas official, and yet another purge within China’s leadership.

    Recent findings suggest that as Russia batters Ukraine’s cities with missile strikes, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has delayed sending scores of Patriot air defense missiles to the embattled country, including those held by European nations, according to a Financial Times report.

    In total, the U.S. has held up around 60 Patriot air defense missiles, including more advanced PAC-3 missiles as well as around 20 PAC-2 missiles. The missiles include those that are already held in European stockpiles but require U.S. sign-off before their transfer.

    Industry observers note that the missile transfers were originally set to occur in September, October, and November in batches of around 10 missiles each. A further delivery is set for December. Ukraine began sounding the alarm publicly in October.

    Patriot air defense missiles are Ukraine’s primary defense against Russian ballistic missiles, which Russia has used in an accelerating campaign to make Ukraine’s major cities unlivable.

    In a recent development, since September, Russia has attacked Ukraine’s energy infrastructure more than 350 times, frequently resulting in days with no regular supply of power or water, a growing concern as winter approaches. The Pentagon is separately delaying approving a proposal to allow Ukraine to produce its own Patriot missiles domestically.

    The slowed deliveries follow interruptions in recent weeks to the functioning of Starshield, a version of the Starlink satellite internet service that Ukraine relies on for battlefield communication. Ukraine uses Starshield in its mid-range strike drones, as well as in systems used to defend against jet-powered Russian attack drones. Starshield is owned by Elon Musk’s SpaceX. Musk and the Trump administration have traded blame over who is responsible for the throttling of Ukraine’s Starshield access.

    Even as Russia scores wins in its missile campaign against Ukraine, however, recently leaked data and Ukraine’s own strikes illustrate the high price Moscow is paying.

    Russia has lost at least 490,000 soldiers, according to data derived from a leaked Russian government database and analyzed by independent Russian news outlet Meduza. Even that may be an underestimate—a further 230,000 are listed as missing in action, many of whom are likely dead but not yet officially recorded as such. That means that as many as 720,000 may have died in Ukraine. The losses place the war in Ukraine as the deadliest conflict for Russia since World War II.

    Russia primarily sends volunteers to fight in Ukraine and pays large bonuses as an incentive. While Russia has so far been able to find enough volunteers to staff its army, the losses are an economic and social strain on the country. Data compiled by Janis Kluge, an expert on Russian recruitment, indicates a slowdown in recruiting for October as compared to last year.

    Meanwhile, Ukraine’s long-range strike capacity continues to develop. On Tuesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that Ukraine was behind a strike on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland. Ukrainian drone also recently attacked a Russian warship docked at a port in Libya. Ukraine on Tuesday separately launched yet another mass wave of strikes on Russia, with Russia stating that it shot down 699 drones.

    Recent findings suggest that deadly airstrikes. Israeli forces have “eliminated” Naim Abu Nahal, the head of Hamas’s internal security apparatus, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz announced in a joint statement posted on X on Tuesday. Nahal took on the role in September, after Israeli forces seized his predecessor in a Gaza ground operation and took him to Israel. “No terrorist will succeed in evading the long arm of the State of Israel,” the statement added.

    The Israeli military also rolled out two airstrikes that killed six other people in Gaza on Tuesday, including a teenage boy and two police officers, who were killed at a police station, according to Palestinian health officials and first responders. Gaza’s police force slammed what it called “an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos,” the BBC reported; Israeli forces stated they struck “military operatives.”.

    Corruption probe. A top Chinese Communist Party official once considered a possible successor to Chinese leader Xi Jinping is being investigated “for suspected severe violations of discipline and laws,” Xinhua reported on Tuesday, in the latest example of ongoing purges of China’s leadership.

    The official, Chen Jining, is the head of the Communist Party in Shanghai, China’s most populous city and a key economic center. He is also a member of China’s Politburo, an elite group of 24 officials that help lead the country. He had been seen as likely to rise within the ranks of China’s government, having previously served as mayor of Beijing.

    The move is part of Xi’s long-running anti-corruption campaign that has seen hundreds of top officials, including many within the military, convicted. Since 2025, three other members of the Politburo have also faced corruption charges, and in the last two months, corruption charges were confirmed against both Beijing’s deputy mayor and the former mayor of major city Chongqing.

    Xi’s consolidation of power comes ahead of a likely fourth term as president beginning next year, meaning that he will hold power until at least 2032.

    Sources indicate that money up front. Japan will pay its full contribution to the International Criminal ​Court (ICC) ahead of schedule following an appeal by the court after the United States sanctioned it, according to Prime Minister Sanae ‌Takaichi.

    Japan is one of the largest contributors to the court, accounting for around 15 percent of its funding. The early payment will give the court a larger financial cushion after U.S. sanctions take effect in April 2027.

    Industry observers note that the Trump administration launched a campaign against the ICC in July, starting with pressuring other nations to withdraw from it. That effort has been largely unsuccessful, with only four countries—Tajikistan, Chad, Venezuela, and Naoero—leaving the court. In October, the United States sanctioned the ICC itself, which U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called a “rogue court.”.

    Industry observers note that the United States has long been concerned about the ICC’s ability to prosecute U.S. soldiers. However, the Trump administration’s pressure on the ICC represents the sharpest attack yet on the body.

    Sunset today will see the appearance of a supermoon, during which the celestial body will be about 30 percent brighter and nearly 20 percent larger than normal. In North America, a full moon that falls after Nov. 7 is known as a “beaver” moon, as it usually occurs around when beavers are building their dams and stocking up on food. If you happen to miss this month’s supermoon, though, don’t worry: There are three more coming in a row in December, January, and February, according to NASA. Happy moongazing!

    • Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., will resign effective Dec.
    • Gomez, who was defeated in his bid for reelection this month, announced his resignation Monday, hours after the Ethics panel released its final report which also said Gomez’s conduct “could constitute criminal misdemeanor sexual abuse.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., pictured leaving the Capitol on Nov. 9, will resign Dec. 1. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., will resign effective Dec. 1 after the House Ethics Committee noted it found “substantial evidence” that Gomez engaged in sexual misconduct with a congressional staffer.

    Gomez, who was defeated in his bid for reelection this month, announced his resignation Monday, hours after the Ethics panel released its final report which also said Gomez’s conduct “could constitute criminal misdemeanor sexual abuse.”.

    Sources indicate that the report was one of four released by the Ethics panel Monday. Three of them are about members who are set to depart the House after the 119th Congress, and the fourth is about the conduct of a former chief of staff.

    In a statement, Gomez said he took “full responsibility for the personal mistakes I committed outside of my marriage,” but that he also had “strong disagreements with the Committee’s report and its conclusions.” Despite his concerns with the process, though, he said he saw no alternative other than to resign because “he was not given an opportunity to respond” to the final report.

    A statement issued by lawyers representing the female staffer with whom Gomez was accused of engaging in misconduct applauded the “thorough and sensitive” handling of the investigation.

    In a recent development, “However, Representative Gomez’s conduct did not occur in a vacuum, and immediate steps must be taken by Congress to rein in what the report describes as a ‘toxic and predatory culture,’” the attorneys, Lisa J. Banks and Sarah E. Nesbitt, added. “Democracy cannot function properly when women must endure harassment and abuse as a condition of public service.”.

    The committee began investigating Gomez after a Upcoming York Post story alleged the congressman was seen kissing a congressional staffer at a party hosted by then-Rep. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif. At the time, Gomez said he did not violate any House ethics rules. Swalwell resigned earlier this year amid a slew of sexual assault allegations from four separate women, one of whom was a former staffer.

    But the more serious allegations addressed by the Ethics probe involve another female staffer, identified in the report as Witness 1. She testified in a deposition with the committee that on one occasion, Gomez touched her genitals without consent at a Washington bar. Gomez remarked in his own interview with the committee that while he did engage in sexual conduct with the staffer, “she did not say no, she did not push me away.”.

    The same staffer, who did not work for Gomez, noted he made inappropriate advances in a separate incident in Gomez’s congressional office, which Gomez downplayed as just a “beso,” or kiss, and hug.

    In its report, the committee determined that the congressional staffer’s testimony “was clear and was supported by evidence that she contemporaneously complained of his conduct” to another witness, and was part of an intolerable “toxic and predatory culture” on Capitol Hill.

    A statement issued by House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and other House Democratic leaders called the report “serious and deeply troubling,” and that Gomez’s resignation was “appropriate.”.

    “Decisive action to set a new standard for reform is an urgent priority for House Democrats,” the statement stated.

    Gomez was one of two House members from the Golden State to lose to a fellow Democrat earlier this month. Northern California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones.

    Industry observers note that gomez faced off against Angela Gonzales-Torres in the general election after both advanced from the state’s all-party primary in June. Gonzales-Torres, a Democratic Socialist and housing advocate, had the backing of several progressive groups, including Justice Democrats and Leaders We Deserve. Her supporters criticized Gomez after the House Ethics panel opened its investigation in August. Her campaign also sought to publicize the inquiry in the weeks leading up to Election Day, The Washington Post reported.

    The committee also released findings of its probes into Reps. Mike Collins, R-Ga., and Troy Nehls, R-Texas, as well as Brandon Phillips, Collins’ former chief of staff.

    Collins, who lost his Senate bid earlier this month, was under review following an Office of Congressional Conduct referral alleging that Phillips hired his girlfriend as an intern. Collins’ lawyers denied the allegations, and Phillips was fired earlier this year.

    Industry observers note that collins and the committee reached a mutual agreement under which he would return $2,880 to the U.S. Treasury after the committee found he had overpaid the “intern,” allowing it to close the case.

    Phillips, who did not comply with his congressional subpoenas, has been recommended by the committee to be held in contempt of Congress.

    It has been revealed that “At no point did Mr. Phillips offer a satisfactory legal justification for his failure to comply with the subpoena,” the committee wrote.

    Sources indicate that the committee probed Nehls for allegedly using campaign money for his personal benefit. Nehls did not run for reelection, but his twin brother, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, will replace him in January.

    The committee found that the Texas Republican “improperly used a manufacturer that he owned as a political committee; the company, Liberty 1776, received and disbursed funds for the benefit of Representative Nehls’ campaign and other unverifiable purposes.”.

    Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Vital Ally.

    Sources indicate that american politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel. On November 3, as Americans headed to the polls, U.S. President Donald Trump made the surprising announcement that the United States would stop sending aid to Israel, valued at around $4 billion annually, by the end of the year. That night, Democrats, many of whom are increasingly outspoken in their criticism of Israeli actions, swept the House and Senate.

    As I wrote in Foreign Affairs a year ago, the “exceptional relationship” between the United States and Israel, in which Israel is treated differently than any other U.S. ally or partner, is coming to an end. No other country receives the tremendous latitude and unconditional backing that the United States extends to Israel. In addition to directly hurting Palestinians, the United States’ support for Israel incentivizes reckless Israeli behavior and dubious strategic thinking. The consequences of the blank check are clear. Over the past three years, tens of thousands of Gazans have been killed, progress toward peace and reconstruction in the Gaza Strip has stalled, the annexation of the West Bank proceeds at an unprecedented rate, and the United States is stuck in an unpopular war in the Middle East with seemingly no end. Israel, for its part, is no safer than on October 6, 2023, and unquestionably more isolated.

    According to recent reports, things are about to change. For better or worse, the United States will recalibrate its relationship with Israel over the coming years and a upcoming paradigm for the bilateral relationship will emerge—one in which Israel is expected to comply with U.S. and international law, the two countries refrain from interfering in each other’s domestic politics, and the United States limits its support when Israeli goals conflict with its own.

    Industry observers note that this change is inevitable, and there is little that Israel and its supporters can do to stop it. But Israel can help keep the United States onside by making itself a reliable partner. As it begins what could be a drawn-out government formation process after last month’s elections, Israel can opt to change direction and plot a course that will not further alienate its closest ally.

    Recent findings suggest that whoever leads the next Israeli government can begin rebuilding trust with the United States before a new U.S. president takes office, in 2029. It won’t be easy. Just as Americans have grown critical of Israel over the past three years, Israelis have shifted further to the right. Israel’s next leaders will need the courage to curb the country’s expansionist policies and resurrect the much-maligned two-state solution. But if they fail to overhaul their approach to Palestinians and the wider region, Israel risks losing its biggest champion and defender—perhaps for good.

    Sources indicate that trump, who seems to delight in bullying U.S. allies and partners, has maintained the United States’ long-standing exceptional approach to Israel. He joined Israel in launching strikes on Iran in June 2025 and a larger war in February 2026, embarking for the first time on a truly joint military operation with the Jewish state. Like other presidents before him, Trump has provided Israel with bombs, missiles, and aircraft, largely with no strings attached. He and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have also interfered in each other’s political systems to an unprecedented degree by endorsing candidates.

    Sources indicate that time and again, Trump has deferred to Israel even when such support has run against American interests. The 2026 war on Iran is the most blatant example. Netanyahu persuaded Trump to give up nuclear talks with Iran and join a war that has failed in its objectives and upended energy markets. Even where the Trump administration has staked out U.S. priorities, it has largely refrained from trying to compel Israel to adhere to them. Israel, for example, has obstructed Trump’s peace proposal for Gaza, which is meant to restore governance to the Palestinians, disarm Hamas, and lead to a permanent Israeli withdrawal from the territory. Israel has undermined the plan by expanding its military footprint in Gaza beyond the agreed demarcation lines and denying entry to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), an interim technocratic body that is intended to govern the territory under Trump’s plan and is at the moment marooned in Egypt. But the Trump administration has barely sounded a single note of disapproval, reinforcing Netanyahu’s long-standing view that he can defy the United States at little cost.

    Moreover, it remains to be seen whether Trump will follow through on his pledge to cut military aid to Israel. The timing of his statement suggests it could have been an electoral stunt, and he remarked himself that the announcement would deprive the left of a talking point. One possibility is that the United States continues gifting Israel weapons to the tune of billions, just under a different guise. The National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal year 2027, which passed the House this summer and could pass the Senate before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress this coming January, contains a provision that would expand the Pentagon’s financial and material assistance to Israel.

    It has been revealed that trump has made no effort to bring U.S. military assistance or transfers to Israel in line with what it provides to other countries. For decades, the United States has been reluctant to subject arms sales to Israel to U.S. regulations or condition them on Israeli behavior. All recent presidents, for example, have effectively exempted Israel from so-called Leahy laws, which prohibit U.S. assistance to foreign military units credibly implicated in human-rights violations. Despite rampant settler terrorism in the West Bank, in many cases facilitated by the Israeli military, the Trump administration has not indicated that it would declare any Israeli units ineligible to receive U.S. weapons.

    Trump has also intervened in Israeli politics more than any other U.S. leader. He has hectored Israeli President Isaac Herzog to pardon Netanyahu so that the prime minister can escape the consequences of an ongoing corruption trial. Ahead of October’s election in Israel, Trump offered Netanyahu a “complete and total endorsement” in his bid for another term. Such blatant interference in Israel’s domestic politics not only undermines the rule of law and integrity of Israeli elections but also serves to normalize Netanyahu’s repeated interventions in U.S. domestic politics. True to form, the Israeli prime minister has praised Trump as “by far the greatest friend Israel has ever had or will have in the White House” just two weeks before the U.S. midterm elections, effectively endorsing Republican candidates for Congress. As in other areas of the relationship, Trump has made what is already an unhealthy dynamic worse.

    Unconditional support from the United States has hurt Israel in a crucial way: it indulges the worst instincts of Israeli leaders and does nothing to dissuade them from their embrace of a near-perpetual state of war. After Hamas’s attack three years ago, Israel has bombed Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and even Qatar. Although Israel has dealt blows to its adversaries, there is no evidence that these wars have made Israel any safer. Iran and its proxies have been weakened, but in the course of fighting, Tehran has discovered the extent of its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz and the global economy and appears even more interested in developing a nuclear weapon. In Lebanon, Hezbollah still poses a threat and is devising new ways of striking Israeli territory. Although confined to a smaller portion of Gaza, Hamas is reconstituting its capabilities and quashing any internal Palestinian challenge to its rule. And in the West Bank, runaway settler violence, the proliferation of illegal Israeli outposts, and the growing threat of terrorism or even a Palestinian uprising have pushed the territory to the breaking point.

    Recent findings suggest that israel has also drifted ever closer to pariah status, isolated internationally thanks to its aggressive tactics. Even the country’s closest historical allies have imposed punitive measures that would have been unthinkable just five years ago. Canada, France, and the United Kingdom, for example, confirmed wide-ranging sanctions against Israeli settlements in the West Bank in September. Such policies are no longer only the purview of traditional critics of Israel, such as Indonesia and Ireland.

    Israel’s reputation within the United States has also tanked. According to Pew polling, 60 percent of Americans have an unfavorable view of Israel, up from 42 percent in 2022. So far, Trump has stopped Congress from restricting support for Israel—both through threatening vetoes and applying pressure on congressional Republicans—but he cannot hold back the tide of American public opinion indefinitely. Once it breaks, Israelis will have to face more than criticism from its closest ally and security guarantor. With Democrats soon to be in control of both the House and the Senate, Congress will likely pass bills that sanction settlement building and condition military aid on adherence to U.S. and international law.

    Without changes in U.S. and Israeli policy, the two countries could see their relationship rupture as continued support for Israel becomes politically untenable in the United States. To rehabilitate itself in the eyes of Americans—and therefore ensure long-term cooperation with the United States—Israel will need to change course. It must abandon Netanyahu’s bludgeoning approach to both the Palestinians and the wider region.

    In a recent development, it is no exaggeration to say that the future of the U.S.-Israeli relationship rests on what type of government Israel forms in the next few months. Netanyahu’s exclusion from the next government represents the best hope for preserving bilateral relations with the United States. Netanyahu has proved unwilling to stay out of U.S. politics or modify draconian security policies that have run afoul of the American public. Unfortunately, most of Netanyahu’s rivals for prime minister share his hawkish position on the Palestinians and the Middle East. Were they in power, they seem likely to resist fundamental revisions to Israeli policy that could safeguard the bilateral relationship.

    It has been revealed that israel’s next leaders need to journey outside their comfort zone. They will have to come to terms with new realities: that tensions between the United States and Israel are now deep-rooted and that they can’t rely on the adamantine support of the Republican party any longer. To win back Americans, the Israeli government will have to rigorously follow through on its commitments under Trump’s proposal for Gaza, daring Hamas to follow suit. In addition to flooding Gaza with humanitarian aid, Israel should let the NCAG enter the territory to offer an alternative to Hamas’s rule and nihilistic agenda. Enabling the deployment of newly trained Palestinian security forces and the formation of the International Stabilization Force, a peacekeeping mission, would also help show that, whatever unfolds in Gaza, Israel is operating in good faith. Israeli forces should immediately return to the demarcation lines traced in Trump’s Gaza peace plan and pull back even further in concert with Hamas’s progress in fulfilling the terms of the plan until Israel has completely withdrawn from Gaza.

    According to recent reports, israel must also rein in violent settlers in the West Bank and hold them accountable through the courts. The Israeli security services can identify the leaders and primary instigators behind the violence and should arrest them and bring them to justice. Given that settlers have killed and injured American citizens in these attacks, continued inaction by Israeli authorities is a recipe for more friction with the United States, especially if a Democratic government comes to power in Washington.

    Industry observers note that israel must also halt its creeping annexation of the West Bank. Over the past three years, the Netanyahu government has increased its military presence in the West Bank, deprived the Palestinian Authority of funds, asserted Israeli government control over larger swaths of Palestinian land, approved a slew of new Israeli settlements, and retroactively legalized illicit outposts. In sum, these actions aim to render a Palestinian state impossible. Although reversing these measures would not arrest the expansion of existing settlements and Israeli infrastructure throughout the West Bank, they would be received positively in the United States.

    In a recent development, israeli leaders also need to break the taboo around Palestinian statehood. Only a couple of decades ago, the idea of a Palestinian state was conceivable to most Israelis. Today, Israeli politicians, with precious few exceptions, cannot bring themselves to endorse a two-state solution. It will take time and no small degree of political resolve, but Israeli leaders must convince the public to accept the necessity and the virtues of a Palestinian state existing side by side with Israel. An Israel that can view Palestinians as neighbors entitled to the same rights would provide a very different image to the world than a messianic government bent on expelling whole populations.

    According to recent reports, these steps will not satisfy all American critics of Israel. Anti-Israeli attitudes cannot be erased in a matter of months. Where anti-Israeli opinion intersects with anti-Semitism—evident in incidents such as a recent boycott of Jewish-owned restaurants in Philadelphia organized by the group Philly Bike on Your Left—the task is even more difficult and will necessitate a different set of policies that transcend Israel, including the formation of diverse domestic and international coalitions to identify and condemn anti-Semitic acts. Yet a far less belligerent Israel and one newly committed to the resolution of the unanswered question of Palestinian self-determination would start to shift U.S. public opinion back in the country’s favor.

    Sources indicate that if Israel fails to change course, it will find itself less secure and more isolated internationally. Without access to international markets and capital, its economy, which has withstood the turmoil of the last several years remarkably well, will suffer and living standards will fall. Under these circumstances, Jewish Israeli citizens with second passports may elect to leave, depriving the state of its raison d’être—providing a safe and prosperous homeland for the Jewish people. Put simply, an Israel without American support will struggle to survive.

    Armenia’s Pivot to Washington

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1517 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that the photographs lining the walls of the stairs of the Armenian Embassy in Washington are impossible to miss.
    • I asked if they change the photographs with each administration, and the embassy’s spokesperson informed me that this is the first time any photographs have been put up—to mark the momentous nature of the Trump administration’s relationship with Armenia.
    • Sources indicate that the photographs lining the walls of the stairs of the Armenian Embassy in Washington are impossible to miss.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    It has been revealed that the photographs lining the walls of the stairs of the Armenian Embassy in Washington are impossible to miss. There are multiple portraits of Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan with U.S. President Donald Trump in the White House last year; pictures of Pashinyan and U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance in Yerevan from February of that same year, when Vance became the senior-most sitting U.S. official to visit Armenia; and photos of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio during his visit to Yerevan last May. There are also multiple pictures of the Oval Office prayer meeting organized by the embassy in September, where Trump met with leaders from the Armenian Christian community in the United States.

    I asked if they change the photographs with each administration, and the embassy’s spokesperson informed me that this is the first time any photographs have been put up—to mark the momentous nature of the Trump administration’s relationship with Armenia.

    Sources indicate that the photographs lining the walls of the stairs of the Armenian Embassy in Washington are impossible to miss. There are multiple portraits of Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan with U.S. President Donald Trump in the White House last year; pictures of Pashinyan and U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance in Yerevan from February of that same year, when Vance became the senior-most sitting U.S. official to visit Armenia; and photos of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio during his visit to Yerevan last May. There are also multiple pictures of the Oval Office prayer meeting organized by the embassy in September, where Trump met with leaders from the Armenian Christian community in the United States.

    I asked if they change the photographs with each administration, and the embassy’s spokesperson informed me that this is the first time any photographs have been put up—to mark the momentous nature of the Trump administration’s relationship with Armenia.

    Trump brokered the signing of a joint declaration in August 2025 between Pashinyan and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev, which committed Armenia and Azerbaijan to resolving their decadeslong violent conflict over disputed territories. It’s one of several wars that Trump claimed to have solved during his second term as he lobbied for the Nobel Peace Prize, though the two countries have yet to sign a formal peace agreement more than a year later.

    It has been revealed that “The final peace deal is not there, but we have peace on the ground,” Armenian Ambassador Narek Mkrtchyan stated. “We have trade relations with Azerbaijan right now—we are buying some stuff from them, they are buying from us—and this is very important for the peace. Of course, there are still some issues that need to be addressed, but in general, peace is in the region.”.

    Monday marked movement on two of the biggest outstanding issues.

    According to recent reports, armenia put forward a draft proposal of its new constitution that removes language calling for reunification with the Nagorno-Karabakh region, a disputed territory within Azerbaijan that was controlled by ethnic Armenians until an Azerbaijani military offensive deposed them in 2023. Pashinyan has supported the new constitution—which Azerbaijan has demanded as a condition to reach a permanent peace deal—and has stated that he will resign if a referendum to adopt it fails.

    The second development was the official launch of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), a roughly 27-mile transit corridor between Azerbaijan and its exclave of Nakhchivan that was agreed (and rebranded from the “Zangezur corridor”) during the joint declaration in Washington last August. The TRIPP corridor passes through Armenian territory and will be controlled by the Armenian government, though it only retains a 26 percent stake in the corridor’s development—the remaining 74 percent will be held by the U.S. government.

    Mkrtchyan, who previously served as the Pashinyan government’s minister for labor and social affairs, was appointed to be the country’s ambassador to Washington in late August 2025, just weeks after the Trump-brokered accord with Azerbaijan was signed.

    “The current agenda that we have with the United States of America, we never had before,” he said.

    Armenia has high hopes from Trump and TRIPP. “It actually has the potential to change the concept of the South Caucasus. Previously, this region has always been associated with conflict, with instability,” Mkrtchyan noted. “This region has the potential to turn into a territory of dialogue, of connectivity, of prosperity, and cooperation, and the TRIPP project is an organic component of this.”.

    Sources indicate that mkrtchyan also corrected me when I referred to TRIPP as a “corridor,” describing it instead as an “infrastructure project route” with “roads, railroads, fiber optics, transmission lines, possibly pipelines.” TRIPP is now “becoming more than a bilateral project” for peace and connectivity between Armenia and Azerbaijan, he mentioned, and will eventually turn into a key trade passage between Central Asia and Europe—entirely under Armenian jurisdiction. “It’s going to be a new global supply chain,” Mkrtchyan said.

    It has been revealed that those ambitions could run headlong into Armenia’s geopolitical reality. The landlocked country also shares a 193-mile land border with Turkey that has remained closed since 1993, when Armenia’s conflict with Azerbaijan first began. “Right now, 80 percent of Armenia’s borders are closed,” Mkrtchyan said, adding that talks to reopen the Turkish border continue in parallel with the Azerbaijan negotiations, “and there is a lot of hope and a lot of potential.”.

    Sources indicate that then there is Armenia’s 27-mile border with Iran that the TRIPP route runs uncomfortably close to. Iran has bristled at the prospect of having a U.S.-led initiative so close to its territory while Tehran and Washington remain at war, and a senior advisor to Iran’s supreme leader warned this week that “if Trump and his allies want to cross this Iranian red line, we will break their legs.” Armenia’s entire railway system is also still controlled by Russia—a legacy of the erstwhile Soviet Union that both countries were a part of—and the once-tight relationship between Yerevan and Moscow has steadily deteriorated thanks to Russia’s war with Ukraine and a perceived lack of Russian support over Nagorno-Karabakh.

    According to recent reports, but those conflicts have only spurred Armenia to diversify from its neighbors and traditional partners by aligning more closely with Washington, according to Mkrtchyan. “This is a fresh reality, and we live in this new reality, but this is our strategic choice,” he stated. “But we were very transparent and open to our colleagues in the region—we told them that this is not against you. It’s not against Iran, it’s not against Russia. It’s first of all for Armenia’s national interests, for Armenia’s security, and for regional cooperation,” he added. “. This is a unique opportunity to transform the region.”.

    Armenia is also hoping to parlay its newfound U.S. links into becoming a technology powerhouse. Earlier this year, a San Francisco firm called Firebird established a upcoming data center in Armenia in partnership with fellow U.S. firms Nvidia and Dell, in a deal that will be powered by 70,000 of Nvidia’s advanced semiconductor chips by the end of 2027. “We want to become a key partner of the U.S. in providing sustainable supply chains for future AI systems,” Mkrtchyan said. That ambition is further bolstered by nuclear cooperation and critical minerals agreements signed by Vance and Rubio during their respective visits this year.

    “Especially after the peace deal, it gave a strong signal to the American companies that right now is the moment to consider Armenia as a platform for cooperation and investment,” Mkrtchyan noted.

    Recent findings suggest that given that our conversation took place just days after a resounding defeat for Trump’s Republican Party in the U.S. midterm election, officially consigning the U.S. president to lame-duck status for the remaining two years of his term, I asked Mkrtchyan how Armenia is thinking about its relationship with Washington heading into a post-Trump world.

    “It’s very natural that at some point, President Trump and the Trump administration will not be in power. It is also natural that in the coming 50 years, only Republicans or President Trump will not be ruling the government, because our agreement with the United States of America—the TRIPP agreement—is for 50 years,” he said, adding that historically Armenia has had “bipartisan friends” in Washington.

    “Of course, President Trump will always be remembered as someone who brokered this peace deal and the Armenian nation is very thankful to him,” Mkrtchyan added. “But we are building our relationships with the United States of America institutionally.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., attends a news conference with members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus in the Capitol in January.
    • A federal judge Monday released more than 160 pages related to the search of Rep.
    • Industry observers note that judge James Boasberg for the U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., attends a news conference with members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus in the Capitol in January. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    A federal judge Monday released more than 160 pages related to the search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home last month, detailing a week-long court effort from the federal government to secure the documents.

    Industry observers note that judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia ordered the documents unsealed Monday as part of a lawsuit brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking to unseal the records related to the search.

    The records unsealed Monday show the government first sought a search warrant in the case on Oct. 2, 10 days before the Trump administration eventually secured the warrant. Dozens of the 169 pages released Monday were redacted entirely. Others contained significant redactions which made much of them unreadable.

    The records show that the presiding judge in the case, U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew J. Sharbaugh, questioned the government about how it would handle the “Speech or Debate implications” of the search.

    The Speech or Debate Clause is a provision of the Constitution which gives sitting members of Congress immunity from being charged or even having to testify about anything dealing with “speech or debate” in Congress.

    The unsealed document says the government does not think the investigation touches on Omar’s work as a member of Congress at all, and engaged in a weeklong back-and-forth with Sharbaugh about what, if any, alterations to make to the search warrant.

    “The United States believes that ILHAN has committed [REDACTED] crimes over decades — beginning long before she was ever in Congress,” one government motion included in the documents indicates.

    Sources indicate that eventually, Sharbaugh granted the search warrant on Oct. 9, seeking records, electronics and a cell phone related to the undisclosed charges. But the warrant also contained an order allowing Omar to assert her speech or debate immunity before the government could search what it seized in the warrant, according to the documents disclosed Monday.

    “But the issue that remains and the issue this Court independently raised with the government after its initial review of the warrant application is whether the search of a sitting Member of Congress’ residence implicates the Speech or Debate Clause. The government says no. This Court sees it differently,” Sharbaugh says in an Oct. 9 order.

    The documents also noted that the government notified the office of the House Counsel, which said there could be no Speech or Debate protection for a member’s private residence.

    The government’s filings in the case suggested that they are looking for evidence of crimes that may have occurred as early as 1980, around the time Omar was born. The documents unsealed Monday do not include the nature of the crimes the government is investigating.

    Separately Monday,  the DOJ opposed releasing information from a second suit filed by Omar seeking return of items taken by agents during the search without further briefing.

    “Ultimately, if the Press Applicants want access to the Separate Docket, the Court should require them to file papers showing why they’re entitled to it,” the filing claims.

    The administration executed the search warrant last month ahead of the elections, drawing criticism from Democrats and outside experts that the decision was made for political reasons. Since the search, administration officials have said there is a criminal investigation into Omar, tied to her immigration into the United States as a child.

    After ruling last week that some records could be unsealed, Boasberg said the press organizations and advocacy group could still seek to unseal more records.
